# No Guarantee: Coherence, Rationality, and Fragmentation

Camilo Martinez Central European University

Camilo Martinez, Central European University; MartinezC@ceu.edu.

Abstract: According to Anti-structuralists about rationality, such as Errol Lord and Benjamin Kiesewetter, incoherence is irrational because it guarantees a failure to respond to one’s possessed reasons. For example, since having sufficient evidence for believing p entails not having sufficient evidence for not–p, it must be unreasonable to hold both beliefs. I argue that one of the most compelling explanations of how incoherence is psychologically possible, the fragmentation hypothesis, undermines this account of why it is irrational. When one’s beliefs are fragmented, there is no guarantee that being reasonable is sufficient for being coherent.

Key Words: coherence, rationality, rational requirements, reasons, fragmentation

## ANTI-STRUCTURALISM

David Lewis once believed that Nassau Street in Princeton ran roughly east–west, that the railroad nearby ran roughly north–south, and that the two were roughly parallel (Lewis 1982: 436). Consider two intuitions about Lewis’s predicament. First, when he held these beliefs, Lewis was irrational: his beliefs were not fully as they ought to have been. Second, at that time, Lewis was irrational because he was incoherent: his beliefs did not fit well together. They were jointly inconsistent. Sometimes holding a single attitude is sufficient to make us irrational, like believing that the Earth is flat or intending to eat the moon. In cases of incoherence, in contrast, we are irrational because we hold a combination of attitudes that do not fit well together (Worsnip 2021: 3–4). Even if each attitude seems rationally permissible on its own, holding them together is rationally objectionable. Why is such incoherence in our attitudes irrational? The following is an influential view (see, e.g., Broome 2013; Rippon 2010; Bratman 2009; Korsgaard 2009; Southwood 2008):

(1) Structuralism: Rationality requires one to be coherent as such.1

More precisely, there is a class of rational requirements that specifically prohibit incoherent combinations of attitudes, such as jointly inconsistent beliefs or means-ends incoherent plans. According to Structuralism, Lewis was irrational because his beliefs violated a structural requirement of coherence. Although this is an influential diagnosis of why incoherence is irrational, many philosophers reject it. They argue that Structuralism is untenable given two further ideas. The first idea is that rationality is “normative,” meaning that considerations about whether our attitudes are rational bear on whether we ought to have them (Worsnip 2022: 393). When we

are irrational, our attitudes are not fully what they ought to be, and we are criticizable as believers and intenders for this failure (Kiesewetter 2021: 1). Usually, this idea is formulated in terms of there being a general normative reason to do what rationality requires—that is, a reason to be rational that applies across all cases:

(2) Normativity of Rationality: There is a general reason to do what rationality requires.2

The second idea is that we seem to have no such reason to be coherent (Kolodny 2008, 2005; Raz 2005). First, the view that we do have such a reason seems to allow for bootstrapping—that is, the problematic detachment of reasons (Kolodny 2005; Broome 2001). For example, if the view is true, then it seems that one can give oneself a reason against believing not-p simply by coming to believe p, since holding both beliefs would be incoherent.3 Furthermore, it is not clear what our reason to be coherent could be. Most candidates apply to some cases, but not all (Kolodny 2005).4 Given these problems, various philosophers endorse:

(3) No Reason to Be Coherent: There is no general reason to be coherent as such.

Recent meta-ethical work on rationality has centered around the puzzle posed by (1)–(3). Antistructuralists, such as Errol Lord (2022) and Benjamin Kiesewetter (2021), attempt to solve this puzzle by rejecting (1). They argue that rationality does not require one to be coherent as such. Thus, they offer a different explanation of why incoherence is irrational.5

First, Anti-structuralists argue that, at bottom, being rational consists in responding correctly to one’s possessed reasons (Lord 2022; Kiesewetter 2021). Reasons are facts bearing on what attitudes one ought to have. Moreover, these facts are reasons one possesses only if one has some kind of epistemic access to them.6 One must be in a position to know them (Lord 2022), or they must be part of one’s evidence or information (Kiesewetter 2021). For example, since this stuff looks and smells like gin, and I want a drink, I have sufficient reason to drink it. Drinking it for that reason is rational—even if the stuff is actually petrol and my evidence is misleading. Second, Anti-structuralists argue that incoherence entails irrationality in the following way (Lord 2022: 27; Kiesewetter 2021: 235–39):

(4) Guarantee Hypothesis: Whenever one’s attitudes are incoherent, it is guaranteed, as a matter of logic, that at least one of them is an incorrect response to one’s possessed reasons.7

In a case like Lewis’s, Anti-structuralists defend (4) as follows: Suppose p, q, and r are jointly inconsistent, in that p and q jointly entail not-r. Logical truth: one either has sufficient reason to believe both p and q, or one does not. If one does, then a plausible reason-transmission principle entails that one does not have sufficient reason for believing r, so one is irrational in holding that belief. If one does not, then one is irrational in believing both p and q. So, no matter what, one is irrational in believing at least one of p, q, and r.8

If (4) is true, then (1) must be false. For in that case, rational requirements of coherence are superfluous (Worsnip 2021: 55). Anyone who responds correctly to their possessed reasons is guaranteed to be coherent. I will argue, however, that one of the most compelling explanations of how incoherence is psychologically possible entails that (4) is, in fact, false.9

## FRAGMENTATION

Lewis believed each of a trio of jointly inconsistent propositions. Granted that his combination of beliefs was irrational, we may still wonder how it was possible for him to manifest this irrationality. How could Lewis hold such patently incoherent beliefs simultaneously?


<!-- Page 3 -->


No Guarantee: Coherence, Rationality, and Fragmentation

Let us begin with Alex Worsnip’s litmus test for incoherence: a combination of attitudes is incoherent if and only if any agent who holds them is disposed to revise them under conditions of full transparency, where this disposition is (partly) constitutive of the attitudes in question (2021: 133).10

Full transparency means circumstances where the agent is “explicitly and consciously aware” of holding these attitudes. Under these conditions, the agent will revise her attitudes. Otherwise, she does not count as having those attitudes. For example, she will either revise her inconsistent beliefs or else these attitudes do not count as beliefs. They may be wishes or hopes or whatever. According to this test, Lewis could hold incoherent beliefs only as long as he was somehow prevented from appreciating their inconsistency. The question is what explains this failure of transparency. One influential idea is that Lewis could hold incoherent beliefs because his mind was fragmented. His beliefs were divided into different “fragments” that became active at different times and in different situations. Sometimes Lewis was guided by a belief that Nassau Street ran east– west and was parallel to the railroad. Other times, he was guided by a belief that the railroad ran north–south and was parallel to Nassau Street. Yet, Lewis never entertained the conjunction of these opinions, at least not until he realized he was incoherent. Given fragmentation, his inconsistent beliefs were quarantined from each other.11

Some influential views of belief entail that our beliefs are coherent in unrealistic ways. For example, various philosophers think that we can understand our beliefs in terms of what possibilities they rule out (Greco 2023; Stalnaker 1984; Lewis 2001). Believing Hazel is on the mat involves ruling out that she’s on the bed or the sofa. On this view, the contents of our beliefs are modeled as a set of possible worlds, namely, those worlds where our beliefs are true. But this entails that our beliefs are fully consistent and closed under entailment, for there is no possible world where p and not-p are both true, or where p and if p, then q are true but q is false. In response to this problem, various philosophers invoke fragmentation to explain the possibility of incoherence in our beliefs (Greco 2023; Yalcin 2018; Stalnaker 1984; Lewis 1982). Our beliefs can be incoherent if they are divided into fragments, each of them corresponding to a different set of possibilities. We might simultaneously hold contradictory beliefs, such as believing both p and not-p, or we might believe p and if p, then q without necessarily believing q, if these beliefs are spread across different fragments.12

Perhaps not all cases of incoherent beliefs are due to fragmentation. For example, if I—a committed atheist—start praying when boarding a plane, the best explanation for my inconsistency is my fear of flying. In this case, my incoherence arises not from fragmentation in my attitudes but from a contextual factor that prevents my stable beliefs from guiding my behavior. In fragmentation cases, in contrast, explaining the agent’s behavior requires positing different stable belief states that guide her action in different contexts (Stalnaker 1984: 83). Lewis was not incoherent because he was afraid, tempted, or biased, but because he believed different things in different situations. In fragmentation cases, our beliefs are fragmented because we have imperfect access to our evidence or information (Elga and Rayo 2021).13 Different bits of information are available to us in different situations, meaning we are disposed to rely on some bits but not others depending on the context. A non-fragmented agent is disposed to rely on his information that p whenever p is relevant or salient. In contrast, a fragmented agent is disposed to rely on this information only in specific contexts or for particular purposes, rather than in every situation where it might be relevant.14

In Lewis’s case, although he knew many facts about Princeton, he could not access all of them at the same time. Instead, some facts were available to him at some times and for some purposes, while others were available to him at other times and for other purposes. We can represent Lewis’s epistemic state using an access table, which specifies the information available to him relative to different purposes or “elicitation conditions” (Elga and Rayo 2021):15

When Lewis wanted to walk to Princeton Junction station, he relied on one body of information that guided him successfully. Suppose he recalled the Princeton University Campus Map, which shows that Nassau Street runs east–west and is parallel to the railroad. Based on this, he walked southeastward along roads perpendicular to Nassau Street. In contrast, when Lewis wanted to bike to Trenton, he relied on a different body of information that also guided him successfully. Suppose he recalled the NJ Transit Northeast Corridor Map, which shows that the railroad runs north–south and is parallel to Nassau Street. Based on this, he biked southwestward along Nassau Street. These two maps, however, were jointly inconsistent.16

## NO GUARANTEE

The Guarantee Hypothesis entails that at least one of Lewis’s beliefs about Princeton was an incorrect response to his possessed reasons. Is this true? Not if he was fragmented. For each of Lewis’s belief fragments, the beliefs in that fragment were correct responses to the information available to him under the relevant elicitation conditions. When Lewis wanted to walk to the train station, he had access to information indicating that Nassau Street ran east-west and was parallel to the railroad. He believed this based on such information. The same is true, mutatis mutandis, for when he wanted to bike to Trenton. Of course, Lewis’s beliefs were not supported by his total evidence—the conjunction of all the facts he had available. His total information included the fact that his two trusted maps were jointly inconsistent. This inconsistency plausibly gave him a decisive reason to suspend judgment. One might therefore think Lewis failed to respond correctly to this reason in holding his beliefs. However, since Lewis was fragmented, this reason was not a consideration available to him when forming and revising his beliefs. The reason involved the conjunction of two inconsistent pieces of information:

•	 I1: The Princeton University Campus Map shows that Nassau Street runs east-west and is parallel to the railroad.

•	 I2: The NJ Transit NE Corridor Map shows that the railroad runs north-south and is parallel to Nassau Street.

Lewis had access to one conjunct at one time and to another at another time, but not to their conjunction. In failing to respond to this reason, then, Lewis does not seem to have been guilty of a rational failure. His beliefs were unreasonable in light of his total evidence, but not in light of the evidence he reasoned from. Let us make this argument more precise. Even if I1 ∧ I2 was a reason that Lewis could, in some sense, epistemically access—that is, it was part of his total evidence, he was in a position to know it,17 etc.—it was not a reason that Lewis possessed. Thus, according to the Anti-structuralist view, this reason had no bearing on the rationality of his beliefs. To see why, consider Errol Lord’s (2022) account of reason possession: one possesses fact F as a reason to φ if and only if one is in a position to respond to F as a reason to φ, where this involves (i) knowing how to use F as a reason to φ and (ii) being in a position to manifest this knowledge.18


<!-- Page 5 -->


No Guarantee: Coherence, Rationality, and Fragmentation

Knowing how to use F as a reason to φ is knowing how to reason appropriately from F to φ. For example, the fact that this fish contains salmonella is a reason for Lois not to eat it, and she knows how to use this reason if she knows how to reason from this fact to an intention not to eat the fish (as opposed, say, to an intention to brush her teeth). However, one may know how to use a reason without being in a position to manifest this knowledge. Lois may currently ignore that the fish contains salmonella. According to Lord, one can fail to possess a reason if one is not in a position to manifest one’s knowledge about how to use it in reasoning. Clearly, Lewis knew how to use I1 ∧ I2 in reasoning. In fact, once he became aware of the inconsistency in his information, he responded appropriately by revising his beliefs. Yet, as long as he was fragmented, he was not in a position to manifest this knowledge. To do so, he would have needed to be in a position where he could reason from both pieces of information to the act of dropping his inconsistent beliefs. However, as we have seen, Lewis was not disposed to rely on both pieces of information simultaneously in reasoning. As a result, he was not in a position to exhibit the relevant pattern of reasoning. Anti-structuralists may want to resist the claim that fragmented Lewis was not in a position to manifest knowledge about how to use I1 ∧ I2 in reasoning. Even if this consideration was not immediately available to him when forming and revising his beliefs, he was not fully prevented from accessing it either. If he had thought long and hard about it, he would have realized that he had inconsistent information. However, even if Lewis was not entirely prevented from accessing I1 ∧ I2, he was not in a position to respond to this reason while fragmented. According to Lord, one is in a position to respond to F as a reason to φ only if one is in a position to manifest a certain disposition—namely, the disposition to φ when one is in a position to know F. This disposition constitutes one’s knowing how to use F to φ (2022: 121).19 Lewis was in a position to know both I1 ∧ I2, yet he could not manifest his disposition to draw the relevant inference because he could not appreciate the relevant conjunction. He could not “join up the dots,” as it were, even if further reflection would have put him in the position to do so.20

Let us grant, then, that there was a decisive reason for Lewis to revise his inconsistent beliefs, one that he could epistemically access, in the sense that it was part of his total evidence and he was in a position to know it. However, as long as he was fragmented, Lewis was not in a position to respond to this reason. Therefore, his failure to respond to it did not make him unreasonable. He responded to the reasons he possessed, and he did not possess the reasons he failed to respond to.

## NO IRRATIONALITY?

Anti-structuralists may resist my argument in a different way. They might concede that a fragmented agent like Lewis is not guaranteed to be unreasonable. However, they may argue that such an agent is also not irrational. Insofar as the Guarantee Hypothesis aims to account for cases of irrational incoherence, fragmentation raises no problem for it. To better appreciate this reply, consider a claim I made at the start of the paper: Lewis’s case elicits the intuition that he was irrational because he was incoherent. But once we explain his incoherence in terms of fragmentation, that intuition may lose its force. If he was responding appropriately to the evidence available within each fragment, why think he was irrational?21

As a matter of fact, some philosophers believe that incoherence in a fragmented agent does not constitute irrationality. For example, Seth Yalcin (2021) rejects what he calls “interfragmentary coherence,” the idea that belief fragments are rationally required to be jointly consistent. He considers and rejects two arguments in favor of this view. First, inconsistent belief fragments might seem irrational because they guarantee false beliefs. When one’s beliefs are inconsistent, at least one of them must be false. However, according to

Yalcin, false beliefs are not necessarily irrational. A person may reason flawlessly but still end up holding false beliefs if her evidence is misleading. Second, interfragmentary coherence might seem to follow from the very concept of belief. Beliefs help make sense of action, but inconsistent beliefs do not seem to allow us to understand what the agent does. If I believe my bathtub is both filled with snakes and not filled with snakes, how do I manage my hygiene? (Bendaña and Mandelbaum 2021: fn. 12). However, according to Yalcin, fragmentation actually allows more of an agent’s actions to be rationally explicable. For example, Lewis’s fragmented beliefs explain his behavior both when he walked to the Princeton train station and when he biked to Trenton. If Yalcin is correct, Anti-structuralists can counter my argument. However, I do not think he is correct. First, while a single false belief need not be irrational, a combination of beliefs one of which must be false seems rationally objectionable. In the former case, the agent holds a false belief because she is unlucky to have misleading evidence, which makes rational criticism inappropriate. In the latter case, by contrast, the false belief is entailed by the structure of the agent’s mind itself, which makes rational criticism seem justified. Second, even if Yalcin is right that fragmentation allows more of an agent’s behavior to be rationally explicable, this does not mean that belief is amenable to inconsistency. Explaining action is just one of the roles of belief. The idea of belief is also—perhaps predominantly—the idea of a state meant to represent the world accurately. As epistemologists sometimes put it, belief involves a commitment to truth. This commitment is clearly violated when one’s beliefs are inconsistent, as it is logically impossible for all of them to be true. Fragmentation helps explain how an agent can be incoherent, but I do not think it justifies incoherence from a normative point of view. We should retain the intuition that, in believing what he did about Princeton, Lewis was irrational.

## WHY BE COHERENT?

The Guarantee Hypothesis is false. My argument for this claim can be summarized as follows:

1.	Some cases of irrational incoherence are due to fragmentation.

2.	In these cases, the agent is incoherent but not unreasonable.

3.	Hence, irrational incoherence does not guarantee unreasonableness.22

If the Guarantee Hypothesis is false, then arguments for it must be unsound. Recall the argument for the Hypothesis in Lewis’s case. For any trio of jointly inconsistent propositions p, q, and r, one either has sufficient reason for believing both p and q or one does not. If one does, then a seemingly plausible reasons transmission principle entails that one does not have sufficient reason for believing r, so one is irrational in believing r. If one does not, then one is irrational in believing both p and q. Now we can see where this argument goes wrong. The reasons transmission principle it invokes does not hold in cases of fragmentation. Having sufficient reason for believing both p and q entails not having sufficient reason for believing r only relative to the same body of evidence or information. Relative to the same body of information, evidence for p is, by the same token, evidence against not-p. In fragmentation cases, however, different belief fragments are associated with different bodies of information. The agent believes p and q relative to one body of information and r (and q) relative to another. Thus, she may have sufficient reason for each of her inconsistent beliefs. If the Guarantee Hypothesis is false, then Anti-structuralist accounts of why incoherence is irrational fail. We cannot explain the rational failure of incoherence in terms of a failure to respond to one’s possessed reasons. Perhaps, then, we must invoke Structuralism to explain this failure.

No Guarantee: Coherence, Rationality, and Fragmentation

As we saw in section 1, Structuralism is the idea that incoherence is irrational because rationality requires one to be coherent as such. In the remainder of this paper, I will argue that the fragmentation hypothesis supports Structuralism. If our beliefs are fragmented, there is good reason why they should be governed by certain structural requirements of coherence.23

Fragmentation looks like a strategy that helps our belief system cope with our cognitive limitations. If we had unlimited processing and memory capacities, we could easily guide our actions with a single, coherent set of beliefs. Since we do not have these capacities, it makes sense for us to have beliefs divided into fragments that operate in different contexts. However, Andy Egan (2008) suggests a more positive reason for our beliefs to be fragmented.24 Suppose we are “Spinozan” believers, meaning our belief-forming mechanisms output fullyformed beliefs, rather than mere candidate beliefs. For example, when you see a red mug, your perceptual system forms the belief that a red mug is before you. You do not need to evaluate its deliverances before believing them, even if you may later evaluate and revise your perceptual beliefs. Egan argues that fragmentation solves a problem specific to Spinozan believers who, like us, have imperfectly reliable belief-forming mechanisms. It is important for us to know when these mechanisms are unreliable. Suppose, for instance, that you have evidence suggesting your vision is unreliable in the kitchen. It is important for you to respond appropriately to this evidence. But if your beliefs were fully integrated, doing so would be impossible. Upon seeing a swarm of bats in the kitchen, you would believe there is a swarm of bats in the kitchen, and you could no longer believe that your vision is unreliable in that context on pain of incoherence. Fragmentation solves this problem by quarantining your beliefs about your own unreliability from the output of your perceptual system. However, while fragmentation solves this problem, it introduces a new one. By protecting our knowledge of when our belief-forming mechanisms are unreliable, fragmentation undermines our ability to detect when our evidence itself is unreliable or misleading. Often, we come to know that a piece of evidence is misleading because it clashes with other evidence in our possession. When we are fragmented, however, we might fail to appreciate this inconsistency. This is essentially what happened to Lewis. If his beliefs had been fully integrated, he would have recognized the inconsistency in his information and avoided forming beliefs based on misleading evidence. As creatures with fragmented beliefs, we need a way to cope with this problem. I suggest that we can do so if our beliefs are governed by a requirement of pairwise interfragmentary coherence. Yalcin formulates it as follows:

(5) Pairwise Interfragmentary Coherence (PIC): It is rationally required that any pair of belief fragments of a doxastic state be consistent. (2021: 162)

The rationale for PIC is as follows: whenever a pair of belief fragments are incoherent, this indicates either that the agent is currently failing to respond appropriately to her evidence—this is the Antistructuralist view—or that she is failing to detect an inconsistency within her evidence. In either case, it is important for the agent to reevaluate her beliefs. Sometimes she will discover that she has not been adequately responsive; at other times, she will realize that her information contains a previously undetected inconsistency. In such cases, she should address the evidence itself—discarding some of it and, if necessary, seeking additional evidence to settle the matter. Indeed, the fact that we sometimes respond to incoherence by suspending judgment and seeking more information is a further indication that the requirement to be coherent cannot be fully explained in terms of reasons-responsiveness. Often, responding to this requirement is important not because we have made a mistake in our reasoning, but because we need to resolve an inconsistency in our body of evidence—for example, by looking for more evidence.

Why does PIC require only pairwise rather than full interfragmentary coherence? Why not demand coherence among all of the agent’s belief fragments? Because doing so would throw out the baby with the bathwater: it would solve the problem of detecting and managing inconsistent evidence, but only by sacrificing the benefits of fragmentation. To see this, consider preface beliefs. In such cases, an agent believes each of the individual claims in her book, while also believing the negation of their conjunction—she thinks she cannot possibly be right about everything she says. Her access table, in such a case, looks something like this:25

Access table for preface beliefs

| Elicitation Condition | Accessible Information |
|---|---|
| p? 1 | Evidence that p 1 |
| p? 2 | Evidence that p 2 |
| ⋮ | ⋮ |
| p n? | Evidence that p n |
| p ∧ p ∧ . . . ∧ p? 1 2 n | Evidence that ¬ (p ∧ p ∧ . . . ∧ p) 1 2 n |

Her belief fragments are pairwise coherent but not fully coherent. While ¬ (p1 ∧ p2 ∧ . . . ∧ pn) is consistent with each individual pi being true, it is not consistent with all of them being true. Resolving the informational inconsistency that could give rise to such a system of beliefs would require the agent to integrate the information she possesses across all her belief fragments—it would require her, in effect, to cease being fragmented. To sum up, the fragmentation hypothesis supports a moderate form of Structuralism, according to which we are rationally required to resolve inconsistencies between pairs of belief fragments. This is significant, as it aligns with the verdict of Anti-structuralists: both Lord (2022: 60) and Kiesewetter (2021: 257) hold that simple cases of incoherent beliefs are irrational, but preface beliefs, though incoherent, are not irrational. A full development of this Structuralist account is beyond this paper’s scope. Still, it offers a promising explanation for the irrationality of holding incoherent beliefs like Lewis’s. According to Anti-structuralists, incoherence guarantees unreasonableness: if we have sufficient reason to believe p, then we do not have sufficient reason to believe not-p, so holding both is irrational. But not all reasons are always accessible; we access different reasons at different times and for different purposes. Thus, our reasons for believing p may not count against believing not-p in contexts where we hold the latter. To the extent incoherence is irrational, it need not be because it is unreasonable, but because rationality specifically requires coherence.

Yet, Watson is not in a position to manifest his knowledge about how to use this reason because he ignores one crucial detail: that the cabby wears Doc Martens. In Watson’s case, his ignorance of this detail prevents him from joining up the dots. In Lewis’s case, it is his fragmentation.

21.	 The force of this reply is also evident when we consider the comparison between Lewis’s and Lord’s Watson cases that I discussed in the previous footnote. Watson does not seem irrational for failing to respond to reasons he does not possess due to ignorance. Why, then, should Lewis be considered irrational for failing to respond to reasons he does not possess due to fragmentation?

22.	 The Guarantee Hypothesis is a universal generalization about cases of irrational incoherence. Hence, showing that the Hypothesis fails in cases of fragmented beliefs like Lewis’s is enough to show that it is false. One might wonder, however, if the Hypothesis holds in cases of incoherence involving other types of psychological attitudes, such as intentions and preferences. I suspect that it does not. There is good reason to think that intentions and preferences are as susceptible to fragmentation as beliefs. However, exploring this idea is beyond the scope of this paper.

23.	 Other proponents of the fragmentation hypothesis have offered alternative reasons for thinking that our psychological attitudes of belief and intention are subject to coherence requirements. Notably, Davidson (2004b) argues that such requirements follow from the constitutive natures of these attitudes.

24.	 Egan’s argument can be understood in the context of Grice’s influential “creature construction” method. According to this method, we can clarify the nature and function of a given psychological trait by showing how it addresses a specific design problem in constructing a creature with psychological capacities similar to ours. See Grice 1974.

25.	 I assume here that the agent’s preface beliefs do not stem from a mistake in evaluating her evidence, but rather from some of her evidence being misleading. Her belief that she cannot possibly be right about everything she says is based on the idea that there must be some inconsistency in her information—one she is currently unaware of.
